outcome: Nothing since 26 January 2024 has settled, or moved a bound on, whether there are infinitely many base-2 Wieferich primes: no third base-2 Wieferich prime is known (only 1093 and 3511), the last search record is PrimeGrid's completion of the search to 2⁶⁴ announced on 29 December 2022 (before the window), and the in-window work is conditional statements, analogues in function fields and number fields, and reformulations, one of which is an AI-assisted counterexample to a function-field conjecture (the Carlitz-Wieferich analogue, not the integer question).
problem_asks: One question, to be answered yes or no: are there infinitely many Wieferich primes? A Wieferich prime is an odd prime p with p² dividing 2^(p−1) − 1. The statement names no base; the name carries base 2 by its standard meaning, and that is the reading used here. The statement asks for infinitude only. It does not ask for the count of Wieferich primes below x, their density, a bound on how far they have been searched for, any other base (Mirimanoff/base-3 primes, or base-b in general), the Wall–Sun–Sun analogue, or the function-field (Carlitz or Drinfeld module) analogues.

events.what_happened: J. H. Silverman, 'Wieferich's criterion and the abc-conjecture', Journal of Number Theory (1988): assuming the abc conjecture, for every integer a > 1 there are infinitely many primes p with p² not dividing a^(p−1) − 1, i.e. infinitely many non-Wieferich primes to base a. Recorded from secondary sources (Wikipedia, PrimePages glossary) and from the 2025 Graves–Weiss paper that restates it; the 1988 paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Conditional on the abc conjecture: infinitely many non-Wieferich primes (for each base a > 1). It says nothing about whether Wieferich primes are finite, and both the PrimePages glossary and Wikipedia say so.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks: whether there are infinitely many base-2 Wieferich primes is untouched.

events.what_happened: G. Guedes and R. events.what_happened: N. Fellini and M. R. Murty, 'Wieferich primes in number fields and the conjectures of Ankeny–Artin–Chowla and Mordell', arXiv:2508.08472 (v1 11 August 2025; v2 11 February 2026, described as the final version). Theorem 1.1: for square-free d > 2, d does not divide the fundamental-unit numerator u iff for some odd prime p | d, ε^(p−1) ≢ 1 mod 𝔭² (𝔭 above p). events.what_happened: D. N. Giraudin, 'A counterexample to a conjecture of Thakur on Carlitz-Wieferich primes', arXiv:2607.15305 (v1 14 July 2026; v2 22 July 2026). Over F_q[T] (q a power of an odd prime p), a monic prime P is c-Wieferich if the Carlitz module satisfies ρ_P(1) ≡ 1 (mod P²). The paper gives an explicit irreducible c-Wieferich prime of degree 5 over F_(19³), with 19 not dividing 5, which contradicts Thakur's 2015 suggestion that every c-Wieferich prime in odd characteristic has degree divisible by p. It also gives a conjectural closed form for a common factor of [5] and M_5 and reports computations with no counterexample over prime fields in a substantial range. Section 6 ('Methodology and use of AI assistance') credits Claude Opus 4.8, Anthropic, with the work (see ai). v2 changed the former Theorem 4.2 to a conjecture; the counterexample is unchanged. The minimality proof and the search method are deferred to a companion paper 'in preparation'.
events.revisions: v1 14 Jul 2026 (9 KB); v2 22 Jul 2026 (9 KB): former Theorem 4.2 (an exactness statement) corrected to a conjecture. Companion paper (minimality of degree 5, search method) in preparation as of v2.
events.delivers: In the function-field analogue (Carlitz module over F_q[T]), one explicit degree-5 c-Wieferich prime with 19 ∤ 5, which refutes Thakur's degree-divisibility conjecture in that setting. It says nothing about the integer Wieferich primes, and says nothing about whether c-Wieferich primes are finite. The paper's computations in prime fields extend the search over a substantial range of degrees and characteristics, with no counterexample found there. Minimality of degree 5 is deferred to the companion paper and is not established in this event.
events.remains: Whether c-Wieferich primes over F_q[T] are infinitely many (the analogue of the question), and everything in problem_asks for the integer Wieferich primes.

events.what_happened: R. Laniewski, 'Radical defects, Wieferich primes, and the abc conjecture', arXiv:2609.00039 (29 August 2026; single version; math.GM). Defines radical excess and 'transgressive' coprime triples a + b = c; for the Mersenne family (1, 2^m − 1, 2^m) an exact defect formula Δ_m = Ω_m + log G_m, where Ω_m collects the Wieferich primes dividing 2^m − 1. The abstract says 'An abc counterexample family along the Mersenne line would require infinitely many Wieferich primes with exponential order defect growth.' Theorem 6.46 (per the paper): finiteness of the Wieferich primes would make the Mersenne line carry only finitely many transgressive triples. The first 100,000 of about 179,000 characters of the HTML were read.
events.delivers: Conditional only. It shows that an abc counterexample along the Mersenne line would need infinitely many Wieferich primes, and that finiteness of the Wieferich primes would limit transgressive triples on that line. It proves no unconditional statement about Wieferich primes, and the exact defect law holds for any primes and says nothing about how many Wieferich primes exist.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, including whether the conditional route to infinitude is ever realised.

events.what_happened: L. Jones, 'Generalized Wieferich primes and monogenic polynomials', arXiv:2609.13904 (12 September 2026): defines a base-b Wieferich prime (odd p with b^(p−1) ≡ 1 mod p²) and extends the monogenicity results for x^(2n) + bx^n + b to N-nomials with N ≥ 4. Full HTML read. The paper states: 'it is still not known as to whether there exist infinitely many' base-b Wieferich primes.
events.delivers: Monogenicity criteria for trinomial and N-nomial families in terms of base-b Wieferich primes. It states that the infinitude question is open and gives no result on it. Discounted.

disputes.summary: Breakthrough Tracker record for arXiv:2607.15305 says 'No substantive AI role was disclosed in the inspected manuscript' and credits no system. The paper's Section 6, 'Methodology and use of AI assistance', in both v1 and v2 of the arXiv HTML, names 'Claude Opus 4.8, Anthropic' and credits it with proposing problems and supplying the computations. I followed the paper, not the tracker. The tracker's own text describes its last check as 29 July 2026 and refers to v2; a search snippet describes the record as version 1; I could not resolve which version the tracker inspected.

arXiv:2609.03091 (Guedes & Machado) is dated 2 September 2026 on arXiv but is a re-posting of a paper published online in Notes on Number Theory and Discrete Mathematics on 16 November 2023. The first public written argument is the 2023 journal version, so the date for this problem's events is 2023, not 2026.

The Fellini–Murty arXiv v1 is dated 11 August 2025, but a search snippet gives the journal's 'received' date as 14 August 2025, after the preprint. The journal page could not be read (the DOI redirected to a placeholder), so the journal dates are unverified.

summary: Question: whether there are infinitely many base-2 Wieferich primes. Finding: no event in the window moves the infinitude question. The only base-2 computational record remains PrimeGrid's search, announced complete on 29 December 2022 (before the window), with no Wieferich prime below 2^64 ≈ 1.8×10¹⁹; I found no later search and no new prime. The 2011 Dorais–Klyve bound (6.7×10¹⁵) is the only other search record I could confirm from a primary source. The window-era items are of four kinds. (a) Analogues: Caruso–Gazda–Lucas (2024), Graves–Weiss (2025), Fellini–Murty (2025), Lucas (2025), Li–Zhao (2026) and the Carlitz analogue of Giraudin (2026); these are about function fields or number fields and say nothing about rational Wieferich primes. (b) Conditional results: Lucas's non-finiteness for Drinfeld modules assumes an unproven 'Conjecture 1'; Laniewski's abc link says an abc counterexample along the Mersenne line 'would require infinitely many Wieferich primes', which points towards infinitude only if that counterexample exists; Fellini–Murty and Graves–Weiss are abc-conditional. (c) Reformulations or uses: Jones (2026, two papers), Falk–Harrington–Jones, Guedes–Machado (the 2023 paper and its 2026 arXiv posting and the 2026 binomial-congruence follow-up), and Cobeli–Zaharescu–Zhang. (d) One AI-involved result on a neighbouring problem. Giraudin's 2607.15305 is a counterexample to Thakur's conjecture for Carlitz-Wieferich primes, a function-field analogue. Its Section 6 names 'Claude Opus 4.8, Anthropic' and credits it with problem selection, domain input and 'the design and execution of all computations'. The Breakthrough Tracker says the opposite; the paper's own text is the basis used here. Whether that involvement is load-bearing is for the later pass; either way the result is a function-field result and does not change the integer question. A separate forum thread for Erdős #11 records that 'I + ChatGPT + Aristotle' worked on that problem in January 2026; it is a different problem and the thread's status changed to 'incorrect claim made'. No AI system is named in any source about the integer question. Close calls: (i) whether the Carlitz counterexample's AI involvement should count at all is a judging call, since it is a different question; I have recorded it in full. (ii) The PrimeGrid bound: a 2021 OEIS-snippet figure of 2.7×10¹⁸ appears in one search result; the later forum announcement (2^64) supersedes it, and I have used the announcement. (iii) The Wikipedia lead's 'about 18×10^18' is a garbled rendering of 2^64 (≈1.8×10¹⁹), which the OEIS comment gives correctly. (iv) Whether the Breakthrough Tracker's denial of AI involvement is a mistake in the tracker or reflects a different version of the manuscript could not be settled from my sources.
competing_reading: Read more generously, the Carlitz–Wieferich counterexample is an AI-involved result about 'Wieferich primes' (the same c-Wieferich condition, the same mechanism), and the authors say the AI supplied the computations that produced it; a reader who counts AI involvement by the authors' own account would record it under this problem. Read more strictly, it refutes a different conjecture about a different object (Carlitz-module primes over F_q[T]), so it changes nothing about the integer question and should be discounted. On the conditional results: Laniewski's abc link and Lucas's Drinfeld non-finiteness could be read as progress towards infinitude, since each says infinitude follows from an unproven hypothesis. Read strictly, neither is a theorem about the integer question. On the 2022 PrimeGrid result: a reader could take it as evidence that Wieferich primes are rare (no prime below 2^64) and so as a reason to expect finitude, but a finite search cannot settle an infinitude question either way.
what_would_settle_it: For the integer question: an unconditional proof of infinitude or finiteness (none found in any source), or a published search that finds a base-2 Wieferich prime beyond 2^64, which would be a new prime. For the AI attribution of 2607.15305: the tracker's correction, or the companion paper's acknowledgements, or the paper's version history showing whether Section 6 was added after the tracker's inspection. For the PrimeGrid claim: PrimeGrid's final statistics page or an independent re-run of the search below 2^64. For the Fellini–Murty dates: the publisher's record (not reached).
